subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term 'urbanisation' mean?
options: The increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas
The movement of people from cities to the countryside
The physical outward spread of a city's built-up area only
A decline in a country's total population
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the growing share of a population that lives in towns and cities rather than rural areas.

questions.q: A megacity is defined as an urban area with a population of at least:
options: 1 million
5 million
10 million
20 million
questions.explain: A megacity is conventionally defined as a city with a population of 10 million or more.

questions.q: A primate city is best described as:
options: Any city with more than 10 million people
The largest city in a country that dominates it and is many times bigger than the next largest city
A newly built capital city
A city made up entirely of squatter settlements
questions.explain: A primate city dominates a country economically and demographically and is far larger than the second city.

questions.q: Squatter settlements in Brazilian cities such as Rio de Janeiro are known as:
options: Favelas
Bustees
Bidonvilles
Kampongs
questions.explain: In Brazil, informal squatter settlements are called favelas, for example Rocinha in Rio de Janeiro.

questions.q: The informal sector of the economy refers to:
options: Jobs that are taxed and officially recorded by the government
Unofficial, unregulated and untaxed work such as street vending
Employment in large modern factories
Government administrative jobs
questions.explain: Informal-sector work is unregulated and untaxed, common in rapidly growing cities in LICs and NEEs.

questions.q: A brownfield site is:
options: Countryside land that has never been built on
Previously developed, often derelict urban land that can be reused
Protected green space around a city
Farmland recently converted to housing
questions.explain: Brownfield land has been built on before and can be redeveloped, reducing pressure on greenfield sites.

questions.q: Counter-urbanisation is:
options: The growth of squatter settlements
The movement of people from urban areas to rural areas
The rapid growth of megacities
Migration between two large cities
questions.explain: Counter-urbanisation is the movement of people out of towns and cities into rural areas.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'push' factor causing rural-urban migration?
options: Better-paid jobs in the city
More schools and hospitals in the city
Crop failure and rural poverty
Entertainment and shopping in the city
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away from rural areas, such as poverty and failing harvests.

questions.q: Which combination best explains why people migrate from rural to urban areas in many LICs?
options: Push: high city wages; Pull: rural drought
Push: lack of rural services and jobs; Pull: better urban employment and services
Push: good rural schools; Pull: farming opportunities
Push: urban pollution; Pull: rural isolation
questions.explain: Migration results from rural push factors combined with the pull of urban jobs and services.

questions.q: Besides migration, urban populations in many LICs grow rapidly because:
options: Migrants are mostly elderly with low birth rates
Young migrants have children, causing high natural increase
Urban death rates are higher than birth rates
Cities steadily lose people through emigration
questions.explain: Migrants are often young adults, so high birth rates produce natural increase on top of migration.

questions.q: Which set of characteristics is typical of a squatter settlement?
options: Wide paved roads, mains sewerage and legal land ownership
Poor sanitation, self-built housing and a lack of secure land tenure
High-rise offices and mostly formal employment
Large gardens and very low population density
questions.explain: Squatter settlements are typically self-built with poor services and no legal ownership of the land.

questions.q: A common consequence of very rapid, unplanned urban growth is:
options: A fall in traffic congestion
Pressure on housing, water and sanitation, leading to shanty towns
An oversupply of formal jobs
A reduction in air pollution
questions.explain: Growth outpacing planning strains services and housing, encouraging informal settlements.

questions.q: Why is the fastest rate of urbanisation now occurring in LICs and NEEs rather than HICs?
options: Most HICs are still largely rural
Many HICs are already highly urbanised, while LICs and NEEs are industrialising with rural-urban migration
LICs have banned migration to their cities
HICs have much higher urban birth rates
questions.explain: HICs urbanised earlier and are near saturation, so growth is now fastest in industrialising economies.

questions.q: Suburbanisation, the outward spread of a city, is often caused by:
options: People seeking cheaper, less crowded housing on the city edge with good transport
A complete lack of transport links
Governments forcing people to live in the CBD
A fall in the total urban population
questions.explain: Better transport and the desire for space and cheaper land draw people to the urban fringe.

questions.q: A site-and-service scheme helps improve squatter settlements by:
options: Demolishing all housing and relocating residents far away
Providing land with basic services so residents can build and improve their own homes
Building luxury high-rise apartments
Banning all self-built housing
questions.explain: Site-and-service schemes supply serviced plots so residents can construct and upgrade housing themselves.

questions.q: One way that improving public transport makes a city more sustainable is by:
options: Increasing the number of private cars
Reducing traffic congestion and air pollution
Encouraging further urban sprawl
Raising fossil fuel use per person
questions.explain: Efficient public transport cuts car use, lowering congestion and emissions.

questions.q: A farming family moves to the city after new machinery replaces farm workers on their land. This is an example of:
options: A pull factor
A push factor
Counter-urbanisation
Natural increase
questions.explain: Mechanisation removes rural jobs, pushing people away from the countryside.

questions.q: In 1990 a country was 30% urban; by 2020 it was 60% urban. This change is best described as:
options: Counter-urbanisation
Rapid urbanisation
De-urbanisation
A stable urban population
questions.explain: A sharp rise in the proportion of people living in urban areas is rapid urbanisation.

questions.q: A city government wants to improve a large shanty town without moving residents away from their jobs. The most appropriate strategy is:
options: Bulldoze the settlement and build a motorway
A slum-upgrading or self-help scheme providing services and legal tenure
Ban all new migrants from entering the city
Relocate everyone to distant rural villages
questions.explain: Upgrading in situ with services and secure tenure improves living conditions while keeping residents near work.

questions.q: A new district is designed with cycle lanes, rainwater recycling, green roofs and solar panels. This is best described as:
options: Urban sprawl
A sustainable urban development
A squatter settlement
Deindustrialisation
questions.explain: Features that conserve energy, water and green space make the development environmentally sustainable.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Urban Environments
